title: Chemical Bonding and Structure
seo_title: Secondary 3 Chemistry: Chemical Bonding and Structure Worksheets (O-Level 6092 with Answers)
standard_code: O-Level Chemistry (6092): Chemical Bonding and Structure
standard_text: Describe the formation of ions by electron loss or gain and the formation of ionic bonds between metals and non-metals; deduce the formulae of ionic compounds; describe covalent bonding as the sharing of pairs of electrons and draw dot-and-cross diagrams for simple molecules; describe metallic bonding as positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons; relate the physical properties of giant ionic, simple molecular and giant covalent substances (diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide), metals and alloys to their structure and bonding (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Chemistry 6092 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 3 O-Level Chemistry worksheets on chemical bonding and structure: ionic, covalent and metallic bonding, formulae, dot-and-cross diagrams, giant and simple structures, diamond, graphite and alloys. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Ionic: transfer. Covalent: sharing. Metallic: sea of electrons.
key_sub: Structure explains melting point and conductivity.
body_html:
How to think about it

Atoms bond to reach a noble gas electronic configuration.

  • Ionic (metal + non-metal): electrons transferred; giant lattice of ions; high melting point; conducts only when molten or dissolved.
  • Covalent (non-metals): shared pairs. Simple molecules have weak intermolecular forces (low melting point); giant covalent structures (diamond, SiO₂) have very high melting points.
  • Metallic: positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons; conducts when solid; malleable. Alloys are harder.
  • Formula of an ionic compound: balance the charges (Al³⁺ and O²⁻ give Al₂O₃).
Example

Formula of calcium chloride?

Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻

two Cl⁻ balance one Ca²⁺

Answer: CaCl₂

Example

Shared pairs in N₂?

each N needs 3 more electrons

Answer: 3 (a triple bond)

Common mistakes

  • Saying solid ionic compounds conduct electricity.
  • Saying covalent bonds break when a simple molecular substance melts.
  • Thinking graphite conducts because it has ions.
  • Forgetting to balance the charges in a formula (writing MgCl instead of MgCl₂).

faq.q: How do you work out the formula of an ionic compound?
faq.a: Write the charges of the two ions, then use enough of each ion so the total positive and negative charges cancel.

faq.q: Why do ionic compounds conduct only when molten or in solution?
faq.a: In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions; when molten or dissolved the ions are free to move and carry the charge.

faq.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
faq.a: In graphite each carbon atom forms three bonds, leaving one delocalised electron; in diamond all four outer electrons are used in bonds.

items.q: What is the formula of calcium oxide?
items.e: Ca<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is CaO.

items.q: Which pair of elements forms an ionic compound?
items.e: A metal and a non-metal.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the N<sup>3−</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 10 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: What is the formula of lithium sulfide?
items.e: Li<sup>+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is Li<sub>2</sub>S.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the Ca<sup>2+</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 18 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: How does an aluminium atom (proton number 13) form an ion?
items.e: Atoms gain or lose electrons to reach a noble gas electronic configuration.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the F<sup>−</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 10 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: What is an alloy?
c: a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements
a pure metal that has been heated
items.e: Steel is iron with carbon.

items.q: Which statement about the ions in magnesium oxide is correct?
c: Both Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have the electronic configuration 2, 8.
items.e: Both have neon's arrangement.

items.q: What is the formula of the ion formed by nitrogen?
items.e: Nitrogen (Z = 7) gains 3 electrons.

items.q: How does a magnesium atom (proton number 12) form an ion?
items.e: Atoms gain or lose electrons to reach a noble gas electronic configuration.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the Li<sup>+</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 2 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: Why do atoms form bonds?
c: to achieve a stable noble gas electronic configuration
items.e: Usually a full outer shell of 8 (or 2).

items.q: What is the formula of magnesium sulfide?
items.e: Mg<sup>2+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is MgS.

items.q: What is metallic bonding?
c: the attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons
transfer of electrons from metals to non-metals
sharing of electron pairs between metal atoms
items.e: Explains conductivity and malleability.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the Na<sup>+</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 10 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: What is a covalent bond?
c: a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms
the attraction between metal ions and electrons
the attraction between oppositely charged ions
items.e: Each atom gains a full outer shell.

items.q: What is the formula of calcium sulfide?
items.e: Ca<sup>2+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is CaS.

items.q: What is the formula of aluminium nitride?
items.e: Al<sup>3+</sup> and N<sup>3−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is AlN.

items.q: What happens in ionic bonding?
c: Metal atoms share a sea of electrons.
Electrons are transferred from metal atoms to non-metal atoms, forming oppositely charged ions that attract.
Electrons are shared between two non-metals.
items.e: Ions get noble gas configurations.

items.q: What is the formula of calcium phosphide?
items.e: Calcium forms Ca<sup>2+</sup> and phosphorus forms P<sup>3−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: What is the name of BaS?
items.e: Name the metal, then the non-metal with -ide. Ionic names do not use prefixes.

items.q: What is the formula of aluminium oxide?
items.e: Al<sup>3+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.

items.q: What is the formula of the ion formed by aluminium?
items.e: Aluminium (Z = 13) loses 3 electrons.

items.q: What is the formula of potassium sulfide?
items.e: K<sup>+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is K<sub>2</sub>S.

items.q: What is the name of K<sub>2</sub>O?
items.e: Name the metal, then the non-metal with -ide. Ionic names do not use prefixes.

items.q: What is the formula of potassium nitride?
items.e: K<sup>+</sup> and N<sup>3−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is K<sub>3</sub>N.

items.q: What is the formula of potassium fluoride?
items.e: K<sup>+</sup> and F<sup>−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is KF.

items.q: What is the formula of strontium nitride?
items.e: Strontium forms Sr<sup>2+</sup> and nitrogen forms N<sup>3−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: Al<sup>3+</sup> and I<sup>−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 1 × (+3) + 3 × (−1) = 0.

items.q: Mg<sup>2+</sup> and Br<sup>−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 1 × (+2) + 2 × (−1) = 0.

items.e: Atoms gain or lose electrons to reach a noble gas electronic configuration.

items.e: Li<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is LiCl.

items.q: What is the name of LiCl?
items.e: Name the metal, then the non-metal with -ide. Ionic names do not use prefixes.

items.e: Name the metal, then the non-metal with -ide. Ionic names do not use prefixes.

items.e: K<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is KCl.

items.e: Name the metal, then the non-metal with -ide. Ionic names do not use prefixes.

items.q: Magnesium oxide has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride. Why?
c: Its ions carry larger charges (2+ and 2−), so the electrostatic attraction is stronger.
items.e: Both are giant ionic lattices.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between iodine (I) and phosphorus (P)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between copper (Cu) and sulfur (S)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between chlorine (Cl) and sulfur (S)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: How many pairs of electrons are shared in a molecule of oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>)?
items.e: Oxygen has double covalent bonds: 2 shared pairs.

items.q: Why are electrical wires made of copper rather than diamond?
c: Copper has delocalised electrons that carry current; diamond has none.
items.e: Copper is also ductile.

items.q: How many pairs of electrons are shared in a molecule of ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>)?
items.e: Ammonia has three single covalent bonds: 3 shared pairs.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between copper (Cu) and gold (Au)?
items.e: Metal atoms share a sea of electrons.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between zinc (Zn) and lead (Pb)?
items.e: Metal atoms share a sea of electrons.

items.q: Why does silicon dioxide have a very high melting point?
c: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken in its giant structure.
items.e: It is macromolecular, like diamond.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between zinc (Zn) and sodium (Na)?
items.e: Metal atoms share a sea of electrons.

items.q: How many pairs of electrons are shared in a molecule of carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>)?
items.e: Carbon dioxide has two double covalent bonds: 4 shared pairs.

items.q: Why does water have a much lower boiling point than sodium chloride?
c: Water is simple molecular, with weak forces between molecules; sodium chloride has strong ionic bonds.
items.e: Only intermolecular forces break when water boils.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between zinc (Zn) and tin (Sn)?
items.e: Metal atoms share a sea of electrons.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between strontium (Sr) and phosphorus (P)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between carbon (C) and iodine (I)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: Why is steel used for building rather than pure iron?
c: Steel is an alloy, so it is harder and stronger.
items.e: Carbon atoms stop iron layers sliding.

items.q: How many pairs of electrons are shared in a molecule of water (H<sub>2</sub>O)?
items.e: Water has two single covalent bonds: 2 shared pairs.

items.q: What type of covalent bonding is in a molecule of hydrogen (H<sub>2</sub>)?
items.e: Count the shared pairs in the dot-and-cross diagram.

items.q: How many pairs of electrons are shared in a molecule of ethene (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>)?
items.e: Ethene has one double and four single covalent bonds: 6 shared pairs.

items.q: Which type of substance has these properties: high melting point; hard; insoluble; does not conduct; used for glass?
items.e: High melting point; hard; insoluble; does not conduct; used for glass: silicon dioxide.

items.q: Which type of substance has these properties: very high melting point; soft and slippery; conducts electricity?
c: a giant covalent substance such as diamond
items.e: Very high melting point; soft and slippery; conducts electricity: graphite.

items.q: Why can metals conduct electricity?
c: They have delocalised electrons that can move through the lattice.
Their atoms share pairs of electrons.
items.e: Properties depend on the particles and the forces between them.

items.q: Which substance has a giant ionic lattice structure?
items.e: Calcium chloride: giant ionic lattice.

items.q: A solid has these properties: very hard, very high melting point, does not conduct. What type of solid is it most likely?
items.e: Example: diamond or quartz.

items.q: Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
c: Its ions are free to move and carry charge.
items.e: Properties depend on the particles and the forces between them.

items.q: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity?
c: Its ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move.
items.e: Properties depend on the particles and the forces between them.

items.q: A solid has these properties: conducts heat well and can be pulled into wires. What type of solid is it most likely?
items.e: Example: aluminium.

items.q: What is the structure of methane?
items.e: Methane: simple molecular.

items.q: Which properties best describe a simple molecular substance?
c: does not melt until over 1700 °C and is made of Si and O atoms all bonded together
hard, brittle, high melting point, conducts only when melted or dissolved
very hard, very high melting point, does not conduct
items.e: Example: menthol.

items.q: Which substance has a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure?
items.e: Diamond: giant covalent (macromolecular).

items.q: Which substance has a simple molecular structure?
items.e: Carbon dioxide: simple molecular.

items.q: Which type of substance has these properties: high melting point; conducts electricity when solid and when molten; malleable?
c: a giant covalent substance such as diamond
items.e: High melting point; conducts electricity when solid and when molten; malleable: a metal.

items.q: Which properties best describe a simple molecular substance?
c: hard, brittle, high melting point, conducts only when melted or dissolved
does not melt until over 1700 °C and is made of Si and O atoms all bonded together
conducts heat well and can be pulled into wires
soft, low melting point, does not conduct
items.e: Example: wax or sugar.

items.q: What is the structure of silicon dioxide (sand)?
items.e: Silicon dioxide (sand): giant covalent (macromolecular).

items.q: Which type of substance has these properties: low melting and boiling points; does not conduct electricity?
c: a giant covalent substance such as diamond
items.e: Low melting and boiling points; does not conduct electricity: a simple molecular substance.

items.q: Why do simple molecular substances have low melting points?
c: Only weak intermolecular forces must be overcome, not the strong covalent bonds.
items.e: Properties depend on the particles and the forces between them.

items.q: Why does sodium chloride have a high melting point?
c: Its delocalised electrons hold it together.
A lot of energy is needed to overcome the strong electrostatic forces between the oppositely charged ions in the giant lattice.
The covalent bonds in the molecules are strong.
items.e: Properties depend on the particles and the forces between them.

items.q: Which substance has a giant ionic lattice structure?
items.e: Sodium chloride: giant ionic lattice.

items.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
c: Each carbon atom uses three electrons in bonds, so one electron per atom is delocalised and free to move.
items.e: Properties depend on the particles and the forces between them.

items.q: Why is graphite soft and used as a lubricant?
c: Its layers are held by weak forces and can slide over each other.
items.e: Properties depend on the particles and the forces between them.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, argon (Ar) or butane (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>)?
c: They boil at the same temperature.
It depends only on the container.
items.e: Both have only intermolecular forces; butane is larger (58 g/mol vs 40 g/mol), so its forces are stronger.

items.q: Why are metals malleable?
c: Layers of positive ions can slide over each other without breaking the metallic bonding.
items.e: Properties depend on the particles and the forces between them.

items.q: Which properties would you expect for silicon dioxide (sand) (a giant covalent structure)?
c: very high melting point; usually does not conduct (graphite does)
high melting point; conducts when solid
high melting point; conducts only when melted or dissolved
low melting point; does not conduct electricity
items.e: Structure explains properties.

items.q: A substance melts at 80 °C and does not conduct electricity. What is its likely structure?
items.e: Low melting point: weak intermolecular forces.

items.q: Which type of substance has these properties: very high melting point; very hard; does not conduct electricity?
c: a giant covalent substance such as diamond
items.e: Very high melting point; very hard; does not conduct electricity: a giant covalent substance such as diamond.

items.q: Which type of substance has these properties: high melting point; conducts electricity when molten or dissolved but not when solid?
c: a giant covalent substance such as diamond
items.e: High melting point; conducts electricity when molten or dissolved but not when solid: an ionic compound.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, ethane (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) or hydrogen fluoride (HF)?
c: They boil at the same temperature.
It depends only on the container.
items.e: Hydrogen fluoride has hydrogen bonds, which are stronger than the intermolecular forces in ethane.

items.q: How many electrons does each atom share in the covalent bond in a chlorine molecule?
c: one each, making one shared pair
items.e: Each chlorine atom gets 8 outer electrons.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, octane (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>) or oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>)?
c: It depends only on the container.
They boil at the same temperature.
items.e: Both have only intermolecular forces; octane is larger (114 g/mol vs 32 g/mol), so its forces are stronger.

items.q: Which properties would you expect for sodium chloride (a giant ionic lattice)?
c: high melting point; conducts only when melted or dissolved
very high melting point; usually does not conduct (graphite does)
high melting point; conducts when solid
low melting point; does not conduct electricity
items.e: Structure explains properties.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, acetone (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O) or potassium chloride (KCl)?
c: They boil at the same temperature.
It depends only on the container.
items.e: Potassium chloride has ionic attractions, which are stronger than the dipole-dipole forces in acetone.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, hydrogen sulfide (H<sub>2</sub>S) or sodium chloride (NaCl)?
c: It depends only on the container.
They boil at the same temperature.
items.e: Sodium chloride has ionic attractions, which are stronger than the dipole-dipole forces in hydrogen sulfide.

items.q: Which properties would you expect for magnesium oxide (a giant ionic lattice)?
c: high melting point; conducts only when melted or dissolved
high melting point; conducts when solid
low melting point; does not conduct electricity
very high melting point; usually does not conduct (graphite does)
items.e: Structure explains properties.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, hydrogen sulfide (H<sub>2</sub>S) or neon (Ne)?
c: It depends only on the container.
They boil at the same temperature.
items.e: Hydrogen sulfide has dipole-dipole forces, which are stronger than the intermolecular forces in neon.

items.q: Which properties would you expect for oxygen (a simple molecules)?
c: very high melting point; usually does not conduct (graphite does)
high melting point; conducts when solid
low melting point; does not conduct electricity
high melting point; conducts only when melted or dissolved
items.e: Structure explains properties.

items.q: What is the structure of graphite?
items.e: Ionic compounds, small molecules, giant covalent and metals.

items.q: What is the structure of silicon dioxide (sand)?
items.e: Ionic compounds, small molecules, giant covalent and metals.

items.q: Which properties would you expect for water (a simple molecules)?
c: very high melting point; usually does not conduct (graphite does)
high melting point; conducts when solid
low melting point; does not conduct electricity
high melting point; conducts only when melted or dissolved
items.e: Structure explains properties.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>) or iodine (I<sub>2</sub>)?
c: They boil at the same temperature.
It depends only on the container.
items.e: Both have only intermolecular forces; iodine is larger (254 g/mol vs 160 g/mol), so its forces are stronger.
